title: Finite Time
subtitle: Spend finite attention deliberately
summary: Pip’s calendar fills while energy, credibility, and relationships run down. Time is only one finite resource. The workshop needs priorities, thinking time, and negotiated scope. Sustainable influence means preserving the capacity to help after this week’s emergency, not promising unlimited effort.

concepts.title: Resource budget
concepts.body: Pip accepts a presentation after an exhausting incident. The calendar has a gap; the energy budget does not. Projects consume credibility, relationships, quality of life, skills, and social capital as well as hours. A commitment can draw down the resource needed for the next difficult task. Pip asks what this request will cost and how that resource can recover before treating an empty slot as available capacity.

steps.text: Pip checks more than the empty calendar slot.
A scheduled hour is only one cost.
Ask how the consumed resource can be replenished.

concepts.title: Prioritization
concepts.body: Pip can do the extra migration work, but should it displace the workshop’s crucial project? Prioritization compares significance, ability to help, constraints, and opportunity cost. A safe slice may fit the quarter where the whole migration does not. Being capable is not enough reason to accept. Pip makes deferred work visible so the team can choose deliberately rather than inherit an impossible queue.

steps.text: Pip makes the competing commitments visible.
Choose a feasible slice aligned with the important goal.

concepts.title: Thinking time
concepts.body: Pip tries to settle a design dispute in the five minutes between meetings. Nothing clicks. Two protected hours reveal the dependency everyone missed. Deep analysis is work even without an immediate code change or meeting artifact. Fragmenting every hour creates hidden execution risk. Pip reserves uninterrupted attention for difficult choices instead of leaving judgment to whatever scraps the calendar happens to spare.

steps.text: Pip cannot solve the dispute between meetings.
The uninterrupted review reveals the hidden dependency.

concepts.title: Sustainability
concepts.body: The workshop asks for one more emergency favor. Pip explains which existing promise would suffer and offers a smaller scope or another owner. Saying no can protect an important commitment. Sustainable influence means help remains available next month, not just tonight. Pip negotiates the trade-off before credibility is spent on a missed promise; a reliable pace serves the team better than unbounded effort.

steps.text: Pip explains what another yes would displace.
The request competes with existing commitments.
Preserve capacity to help beyond the immediate emergency.

misconceptions.claim: a staff-plus role is mainly about applying a universal formula.
misconceptions.correction: The chapter treats judgment as contextual: identify forces, listen to evidence, and adapt the response to the actual system and people.

misconceptions.claim: A visible activity or artifact proves the work is complete.
misconceptions.correction: Completion requires a useful outcome, shared understanding, and a way to notice whether the decision worked over time.

scenario.title: Protect finite resources
scenario.context: Pip faces a migration, incident recovery, and a new teammate to onboard. The workshop’s date is fixed, but the migration scope can change.

options.label: Reduce scope
options.benefit: Pip can protect recovery and deliver the most valuable slice.
options.consequence: The workshop agrees a bounded migration and clear delegation. Energy and credibility remain available for the handoff.

options.label: Work nights to keep scope
options.benefit: The original scope stays on the calendar.
options.cost: Night work consumes recovery and raises delivery risk.
options.consequence: Pip may hold the date, but quality of life and future capacity suffer. The next hard decision gets less attention.

scenario.debrief: A fixed date does not create infinite capacity. Pip makes the scope trade-off explicit before the team pays for an impossible promise.

quiz.question: What can a commitment consume besides calendar time?
options: Nothing if the work is interesting
quiz.explanation: The chapter treats several personal and organizational resources as finite.

quiz.question: A useful but low-impact request would displace a crucial project. What is a reasonable response?
options: Explain the trade-off and negotiate scope or another owner
Accept it and hide the extra work
quiz.explanation: Prioritization makes opportunity cost visible and allows a deliberate choice.

quiz.question: Why reserve thinking time?
quiz.explanation: Uninterrupted analysis supports judgment that cannot reliably happen between meetings.

exercise.title: Make the next move legible
exercise.prompt: Describe a staff-level decision, the people and terrain involved, and the route by which you will learn whether it worked.

fields.label: What can be reduced or delegated?
fields.placeholder: State the choice and its trade-off.

fields.label: What protects future capacity?
fields.placeholder: Name the evidence or conversation that will revisit it.
